fig9_1: Two side-by-side panels of the same Gaussian-modulated cosine, u of x equals e to the power minus x squared times cosine of three x. The left panel plots u against position x in physical space, showing an oscillatory wavepacket confined under a bell-shaped envelope that decays toward zero for large absolute x. The right panel plots the magnitude of the Fourier transform against wavenumber k on a logarithmic vertical axis, showing two peaks near k equals plus and minus three and a rapid drop-off away from them, illustrating that this smooth function has a fast-decaying spectrum.
tbl9_1: Table listing fundamental Fourier-transform properties, pairing each physical-space operation (linearity, translation, modulation, differentiation, convolution, multiplication) with its simpler Fourier-space counterpart, highlighting that differentiation becomes multiplication by i times k.
tbl9_2: Table comparing physical and Fourier variables across three settings (continuous functions, the infinite grid of spacing h, and a periodic grid of N points), showing that discreteness in physical space bounds the wavenumber range while periodicity in physical space makes wavenumbers discrete.
fig9_2: Schematic of the infinite uniform grid, a horizontal line carrying a row of evenly spaced filled dots labeled by their indices from x sub minus five through x sub five, with the constant separation marked as grid spacing h. It depicts sampling the real line at points x sub j equal to j times h.
fig9_3: Two sine waves of very different frequency plotted over position x, sine of pi x drawn solid and sine of nine pi x drawn dashed, sampled on a grid of spacing one quarter. Although the two continuous curves look completely different, the black sample dots lie exactly on both curves at every grid point, demonstrating that wavenumber nine pi aliases to pi because they differ by two pi over h.
fig9_4: Three stacked panels showing band-limited sinc interpolation of grid functions with spacing one. The top panel plots a single Kronecker delta spike and its smooth sinc-function interpolant with decaying side lobes. The middle panel plots a discrete square wave whose interpolant overshoots and ripples near the jumps, the Gibbs phenomenon. The bottom panel plots a discrete triangular hat function whose interpolant is smoother but still shows mild oscillations, illustrating that interpolation quality tracks the underlying smoothness.
tbl9_3: Table mapping FFT index conventions for even N across MATLAB one-based indices, Python zero-based indices, and the mathematical wavenumber k, identifying which entries hold the constant mean, positive modes, the Nyquist mode, and negative modes.
tbl9_4: Table of the maximum error in the FFT-based spectral derivative of e to the power sine x for grid sizes N from four to thirty-two, showing the error plunging from about ten to the power minus one to machine precision near ten to the power minus fifteen, the signature of exponential spectral convergence for analytic functions.
fig9_5: Stem or bar plot of the FFT magnitude spectrum of sine of seventeen x sampled at thirty-two points, with wavenumber k on the horizontal axis spanning the resolved range. Instead of a peak at the true frequency seventeen, which lies above the Nyquist limit of sixteen, a single dominant spike appears at k equals minus fifteen, since seventeen wraps around to minus fifteen plus thirty-two.
fig9_6: Scatter plot of sine of n for integer n running from one to three thousand, with n on the horizontal axis and the sampled value on the vertical axis. Although the underlying sequence oscillates by nearly one radian per step, the plotted points group into a slowly varying band of overlapping sinusoidal stripes, an illusory low-frequency envelope produced because the eye undersamples the rapid oscillation.
fig9_7: Three side-by-side spectra of periodic functions of differing smoothness. The left panel, on a semilog scale, shows the coefficients of the analytic function e to the power sine x falling on a straight line, indicating exponential decay. The center panel, on a log-log scale, shows the continuous hat function decaying as a power law of slope about minus two. The right panel, also log-log, shows the discontinuous square wave decaying more slowly as a power law of slope about minus one, confirming that lower regularity gives slower spectral decay.
tbl9_5: Table linking smoothness classes to their characteristic Fourier decay rates, contrasting analytic functions that decay faster than any power, continuous-but-cornered functions decaying like the inverse square of the wavenumber, and discontinuous functions decaying like the inverse of the wavenumber.
fig9_8: Two stacked panels demonstrating zero-padding interpolation of e to the power sine x from thirty-two coarse samples up to one hundred twenty-eight points. The top panel overlays the true function (dashed), the zero-padded interpolant (solid), and the coarse samples (circles), all visually coincident. The bottom panel plots the pointwise absolute error on a logarithmic vertical axis, hovering near machine precision around ten to the power minus fourteen, confirming essentially exact interpolation for this analytic function.
tbl9_6: Quick-reference table summarizing the forward and inverse Fourier transforms and their variable ranges for the continuous, semidiscrete, and discrete settings developed in the chapter.
